deep.reconstruction:
Context (previous page, f.16r). T is a plane region and u a function minimising the Dirichlet integral Ω(v)=∫∫_T (v_x^2+v_y^2) dx dy among all v with given boundary values. M=Ω(u) is the minimum. Put v=u+σ (later u+kσ) with σ=0 on the boundary ∂T. Integration by parts gives
 Ω(u+kσ) − M = −2k ∫∫ Δu·σ dx dy + k^2 ∫∫ |∇σ|^2 dx dy.
The boundary term −2k∮ (∂u/∂p) σ ds, with p the normal, vanishes because σ|∂T=0. Riemann then argues that for small k the linear term dominates the quadratic one. So Ω−M would take the sign of the linear term, which must therefore vanish for every admissible σ.

This page, step by step.
(1) Laplace's equation. Suppose Δu=u_xx+u_yy were nonzero in some part of T. One could then give s (=σ) the same sign as Δu everywhere there (and make it vanish elsewhere and on ∂T). Then −2k∫∫Δu·s<0 for small k>0, so Ω(u+ks)<M, contradicting minimality. Hence Δu=0 in T: u satisfies the second-order condition. [My gloss: this is the fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations. A concrete choice is s=φ·Δu with φ≥0 a cutoff vanishing on ∂T.]
(2) Exact expansion. With Δu=0 and s|∂T=0, for every admissible variation v=u+s:
 Ω(u+s) = Ω(u) + ∫∫ (s_x^2+s_y^2) dx dy.
The cross term vanishes exactly, with no smallness assumption on s. Riemann wrote and then struck out the first term ∫∫(u_x^2+u_y^2), leaving '+∫∫|∇s|^2'.
(3) Uniqueness of the minimiser. If Ω also attained its minimum M at some v≠u, then ∫∫|∇s|^2=0. Hence s_x=s_y=0 everywhere, so s is constant; since s=0 on the boundary, s≡0.
(4) Conclusion (the Dirichlet principle in the form of his 1851 dissertation). The function u can always be determined, and in only one way, so that inside T it satisfies u_xx+u_yy=0 and on the boundary it takes arbitrarily prescribed values. 'Always' rests on the tacitly assumed existence of a minimiser.
(5) Start of the 3-D analogue. Riemann begins to restate a theorem 'in der Lehre ...' which, it seems, 'Gauss ... bewiesen hat'. The theorem essentially amounts to this: a function V of the three rectangular coordinates x, y, z is completely determined in a bounded region (of arbitrary shape: 'es ist ... nicht wesentlich, welche Gestalt/Ausdehnung er hat') if V_xx+V_yy+V_zz=0 there and V has given boundary values. The sentence breaks off. This points to Gauss's 1840 'Allgemeine Lehrsätze ... im verkehrten Verhältnisse des Quadrats der Entfernung wirkenden Anziehungs- und Abstossungskräfte', where a minimisation argument of the same type is used.

Purpose: a draft of the variational existence/uniqueness argument for boundary value problems of the Laplace equation. This argument underlies §§16–18 of Riemann's dissertation (1851) and his later 'Dirichlet principle' (Abelsche Functionen 1857). The next page continues with remarks on variational principles for boundary conditions, e.g. the elastic plate.
errors: Existence of a minimising u is assumed without proof. The infimum of the Dirichlet integral need not be attained in the admissible class (the gap pointed out by Weierstrass 1870, closed by Hilbert 1900). So 'immer' (always) is not justified by this argument; only uniqueness and the necessity of Δu=0 are.
Step 'Δu≠0 somewhere ⇒ choose s of the same sign' tacitly needs continuity of Δu, so that it is nonzero on an open set, plus a smooth admissible s. These are standard tacit regularity assumptions.
'∫∫|∇s|^2=0 ⇒ ∇s≡0 ⇒ s≡0' needs s continuous (C^1) and T connected (or s vanishing on the boundary of each component). This is fine under the usual assumptions.

Previous page: the boundary term '−2∫(∂u/∂p) σ dx dy' is written with dx dy where it should be ds (it is written correctly as ds in the earlier line). It vanishes anyway since σ=0 on the boundary. In the final expression for Ω−M, the bracket 'Δ' is written only as ∂²u/∂x² (an incomplete term), a slip.

results.what: Vanishing of the first variation of the Dirichlet integral with fixed boundary values forces Δu=0 (Euler–Lagrange equation via a sign-choice argument).
results.modern_name: Euler–Lagrange equation for the Dirichlet energy / fundamental lemma of calculus of variations
results.usually_credited_to: Euler, Lagrange (general method); for the Laplace case Green 1828, Gauss 1840, Thomson 1847, Dirichlet (lectures)

results.what: Exact identity Ω(u+s)=Ω(u)+∫∫|∇s|^2 for harmonic u and s=0 on the boundary, giving uniqueness of the minimiser and of the Dirichlet problem solution.
results.modern_name: Energy identity / uniqueness for the Dirichlet problem

results.what: Existence-and-uniqueness statement: a harmonic function in T with arbitrary prescribed boundary values exists and is unique, derived from minimising the Dirichlet integral.
results.usually_credited_to: Named by Riemann (1857) after Dirichlet; Riemann's dissertation 1851; Gauss 1840 and Thomson 1847 had similar arguments

results.what: Beginning of the 3-D analogue for V(x,y,z) in a bounded region, referred to a theorem (apparently of Gauss) in potential theory.
results.modern_name: Dirichlet problem in R^3 / Gauss's 1840 minimisation theorem

deep.surprise_reason: This is a draft of the Dirichlet-principle argument that Riemann published in his 1851 dissertation (§§16–18) and used in 1857. It matches the known content, including the gap about existence of a minimiser. Its only interest is as an early working draft (c.1850) showing the sign-choice argument and the explicit reference to the 3-D Gauss theorem.

checkable.asserts: Cross term vanishes (=0) for harmonic u and s vanishing on the boundary of the unit square.

checkable.sympy: x,y,k=symbols('x y k'); u=x**2-y**2; s=x*(1-x)*y*(1-y); O=lambda v: integrate(diff(v,x)**2+diff(v,y)**2,(x,0,1),(y,0,1)); simplify(O(u+k*s)-O(u)-k**2*O(s))

checkable.asserts: Integration by parts ∫∫∇u·∇s = −∫∫Δu·s when s=0 on the boundary (result 0), for non-harmonic u.

checkable.sympy: x,y,k=symbols('x y k'); u=x**2+y**2; s=x*(1-x)*y*(1-y); O=lambda v: integrate(diff(v,x)**2+diff(v,y)**2,(x,0,1),(y,0,1)); solve(diff(O(u+k*s),k),k)
checkable.asserts: For non-harmonic u, Ω(u+ks) is minimised at some k≠0 (k=12), so u is not a minimiser (illustrates the sign argument).

transcription_corrections: Line 1: read 'in irgend einem Theile von T von Null verschieden'. The region letter T is visible after 'von'.
Lines 2–3: the sense is 'so könnte, wenn man s überall das[selbe Zeichen wie Δu] geben ...'. The marginal word at the start of line 3 is 'geben', not '{+gilt+}'.
Line 3 right: 'Die Function u genügt also der Bedingung, daß der Ausdruck zweiter Ordnung = 0' is plausible. The word read 'Ausdruck' may be 'Differentialausdruck'.
'[-Hätte-] {+Sollte+} nun Ω auch für irgend einen andern Werth von v als u ... seinen kleinsten Werth M an[nehmen]': the transcription is fine apart from the missing 'nehmen'.
The first struck-out integral in the Ω line is ∫∫((∂u/∂x)^2+(∂u/∂y)^2)dxdy, so the surviving expression is Ω = [M] + ∫∫|∇s|^2.

Lower paragraph: likely '... welchen Gauss [...] bewiesen hat, kommt im Wesentl. darauf hinaus, daß eine Function V von den drei rechtwinkligen Coordinaten x,y,z in einem ... begrenzten Raume völlig bestimmt ist wenn sie [ΔV=0 ...]'. 'welcher Grenze' should probably read 'welchen Gauss'. The opening 'Der Satz in der Natur d. h. Lehre des unregelmäßigen Raumes' is doubtful; probably 'Der Satz in der Lehre d. ... im umgekehrten Verhältniss ...', alluding to Gauss 1840.
'Es ist aber nicht wesentlich' has an insertion above ('nicht' / 'nur'). It probably concerns the shape/extent of the region ('welche Gestalt/Ausdehnung er hat') being inessential.
The final formula is ∂²V/∂x² + ∂²V/∂y² + ∂²V/∂z² (the last denominator is ∂z², not ∂y²). The sentence is unfinished, presumably '= 0 ist und an der Begrenzung gegebene Werthe annimmt'.
